has, how many are gaps, and how you
compare with the hub's leader. You can
expand a hub to see every topic in it.
Topics where you rank in the top 20,
topics where you rank in the top 20 are
marked in green.
For the rest you can see the topic's
importance, where you rank, where up to
three competitors rank,
and what you've already started, a
brief, a draft, or even a published
page. Each topic you don't rank for has
one next step.
Create brief starts a brief for a topic
with nothing yet. Create draft turns a
ready brief into a draft. Continue draft
and edit article open the work you've
already started. So silo analysis
updates every time your topical
authority scores recalculate or you've
refreshed the SERPs. And last updated
shows when the last time that happened.

metadata.author: Koray Tuğberk GÜBÜR
metadata.shortDescription:
YMYL SEO involves Your Money or Your Life SEO efforts by providing trust signals to search engine algorithms. Search engines have different algorithms for websites in YMYL niches such as health, finance, and e-commerce. The Topical Authority is only one of the YMYL Trust signals for overall real-world business signals and ranking prioritization. The web sources need to provide brand-search demand and overall comprehensiveness for the usefulness of information on the web source while providing local business signals. The EEAT with Semantics, a case study project, provides a rehab center in Thailand and Sri Lanka to use doctors and Ph.D. researchers as authors. The project leverages the authority of doctors from different industries. 

Using entities for indexation and exceeding the quality thresholds is an effort to the approval of the authority. The search engines might skip some web sources according to their overall relevance to a topic based on a collection of web documents. In other words, even if a web source has 99 quality documents, if the 100th misses some of the entities, the information graph might have critical missing components, relations, and extractions. Thus, the web sources can see gradual ranking decreases due to missing contexts and relations. The case study project demonstrates the importance of a site-wide conceptual relevance check. Ideally, having more than 10 pages relevant to a fundamental industry concept is better. This way, the source attributes its relevance to a topic and creates neighborhood content relations. 

The case study for EEAT and YMYL with topical authority explains how to use competitor analysis to better understand entity-oriented search. The website is compared to other web sources regarding relevance and sentence structures, along with possible cannibalization or hierarchy-based relevance configuration in a semantic content network.

The case study explains the importance and fundamental effect of entity-attribute and context relations. Website structuring and information tree styles are compared to the search engines' perception of macro and micro contexts. The web source is explained separately by Google and Microsoft Bing. The web source is checked via Microsoft Bing's vision, and Microsoft Edge is used to understand the referrer domains, traffic data, popularity changes, and brand reputation. Thus, it is demonstrated that SEOs can leverage even web browsers from different web search engine companies such as Microsoft or Alphabet to understand the overall authority and quality.

The YMYL SEO should involve perspectives with different types of experiences in the field of health niche. For example, it is not only about explaining the main topic, such as addictions for rehab centers, but it is also about explaining and empathizing with the patient from the point of view of a wife, husband, mother, or father. Thus, an experience transfer with perspective-rich content is vital to harmonizing expertise and experience. This does't mean that you should not give facts, it means that you should involve experiences and opinions with loyalty to the factual concepts and information. For example, addiction to a specific harmful substance might be explained by its effect on the blood content, and it can be presented with the impact of the blood content on the mood of the person. This mood change can reflect exhaustion or weakened eyesight. The point is the definition, and experience should be reflected together.

The factual accuracy matters in the YMYL and EEAT SEO. The facts are not coming from directly the real-world, it comes from the consensus. If you are not authoritative enough in the health industry, please protect your alignment with the existing high-level authority sources. Do not contradict with the established authorities, but be better in terms of contextual richness, semantic entailment, and easiness of being understood by the algorithms.

metadata.title: From 0 to 4.000 Clicks a Day: Semantic SEO for Finance - Learn Real Topical Authority
metadata.author: Koray Tuğberk GÜBÜR
metadata.shortDescription:
This case study revisits a finance SaaS website that became cash-positive using SEO alone, without backlinks or external page rank. Despite a long period of inactivity affecting crawl stats, the site retained its rankings and later saw a surge in clicks and impressions. This highlights how Google's processing time and topical authority influence long-term SEO performance.

A key takeaway is the impact of response time on crawl efficiency. The site had 60,000 daily crawls but lost traction when response times increased. Optimizing it to 30-40ms improved indexing. Google's ranking mechanisms, like RankBrain, prioritize structured content and engagement. By refining entity relationships and avoiding templated content risks, the site maintained steady growth, proving the value of consistent SEO and technical optimization.

metadata.title: Digital PR Link Building - 50 Links Built in 3 Hours
metadata.author: Fery Kaszoni
metadata.shortDescription:
Reactive link building at its best.

3 hours of work on Saturday got me the most powerful backlinks and coverage in the world from some of the planet’s most reputable publications:

Telegraph - DR 92

Standard UK - DR 89

Bloomberg - DR 92

The Sun - DR 90

Electrek - DR 80

Yahoo - DR 91

MSN - DR 92

... and many many more.

The campaign went viral and it got covered by almost every major news publication in the UK and around the world, getting our client CarGuide some of the most powerful links you can ever imagine.

All of that, with a quick reactive campaign with simple Google Trends research, around the fuel shortage crisis.

I reveal everything that I've done in this video, including the email that I've sent out to the journalists.

I hope this will inspire you to think outside the box, and show you that big links can be earned with a bit of creativity and the right approach.

segments.text: Back links and coverage on Bloomberg, The Sun, Telegraph, Express, Standard UK, and
it only took me three hours of work. Let me show you exactly how I’ve done it. I will
even share with you the email that I’ve sent to the journalist, the exact pitch.
So, let’s jump on my screen and let’s see exactly how I’ve done it.
So, the research was quite simple, all I have to do is just go to Google trends and put
in ‘Electric Car’ and search for it. It was, like, 30 second’s research. That’s
all the research needed for this campaign. Then the data has shown me that there’s
been a massive hike in searches for electric cars because of the fuel shortage. So People
were disappointed by not having petrol in their tank and they were looking for an alternative
solution. And everyone was looking for electric cars, as you can see here there’s a massive
spike. The actual data for seven days back then was even more spectacular. When I’ve
done the research on the 25th, this was a Saturday, there was a massive spike on the
24th. So, the data was showing quite a spectacular hike in online searches for electric car keywords.
This chart is a story. This is a story that got all of these backlinks.
So, what I’ve done is I took this screenshot, attached it to an email, and I composed just
a simple email saying, look, this is what we’ve found, this is what our client CarGuide.co.uk
has found, and we’ve added an expert commentary on the situation. Let me show you how the
email looks like.
This is how the email looks like, it’s so simple. We just said ‘hey Michael’, or
‘hey journalist’s name’, analysis of google set data reveals online searches for
electric cars exploded 1600%, which is like 16 times on the 24th of September, as you
can see on this chart. This chart reflects exactly what I put in the email and we just
say ‘new finding by our client reveals that online interest skyrocketed and that we’ve
added like an expert commentary from our client of the situation and then we added some really
good factual stats about electric car registrations in August, we put in the sources, and then
we further commented on it. Then I just say, ‘if you need anything else do feel free
to get in touch’. We’ve attached two images here and happy days. That’s all. That’s
the whole campaign. It literally took me like probably one hour to do the research and to
craft this little email, I just had to rewrite it like two or three times until I thought
it was good to go. And that’s the whole execution of the campaign before the outreach.
Now, let’s look at the outreach process. I will show you exactly how I found the journalists
and how we created the list with Roxhill. Let’s jump over to my other screen and see
exactly how I’ve done it.
So, this is Roxhill. Roxhill is a media database where you can find journalists, relevant journalists,
and we can export their email addresses and their contact details, so we can export them
from here and then import them into buzzstream. Let me just show you how we do it.
So, what I’ve done is I just went to ‘Simple Search’, I just put in, so I’ve created
three lists for this campaign. One of them was personalised, more personalised list where
I just put in the key word ‘fuel shortage’, so whenever a journalist talks about fuel
shortage, Roxhill will find the journalist for us and what I’ve also done I’ve made
sure I select the date as the journalists who wrote about fuel shortage in the past,
I think I’ve done it in the past two weeks or three weeks, so that we are like fresh,
fresh data, fresh journalists there who I knew they are talking about it.
So we have, like, 200 journalists, I just download it from here in a simple spreadsheet
like this. I went onto buzzstream, I created a new list, I imported the journalists in
here, and then I just sent out this email to them. Let me just show you, these are like
the journalists, we have like 200 journalists here who we know that they talked about fuel
shortage in the past two or three weeks. Which were like the exact journalists who we know
might be interested in this story. This is like an extra angle to their story and they
can further add value to their readers by showing that electric cars have had like a
massive spike in searches. Now we imported that list here and sent out like 200 emails
to the journalists.
Then what I’ve done is I also went to the publications, the outlets filter and I’ve
chosen the sector which was transport and autos and I’ve got in touch with about 260
automotive blogs. It’s the same, we can export, export the details, all the magazines
and then we have like their email address here. Again I just imported that list in here
and then I reached out to all of these websites. I sent out, again, like a few hundreds of
emails.
And then the third list is where I went on a manually create- googled car publications
and found some of them were not in this list so I created another manual list which you
can find here so let’s- that was all the work I have done. I sent this out, it was
a three hour – three hours ish work on Saturday afternoon. Really good fun, it got us lots
of coverage like crazy coverage.
I hope this story gives you inspiration and it just gives you drive to build better backlinks.
As you’ve seen, you don’t need massive resources all the time. There might be niches
and then in most cases you do have to do more research but this is yet another testimony
that sometimes even with a simple research with a simple story, you can land massive
links.
I hope you find this useful. Let me know in a comment if you have any other questions
and I’m happy to answer them. Have a great day, or a great evening. See you soon.

Digital PR seems to be all the hype right now. But how can we use it for SEO? Can it help us get backlinks? We talk about that and a lot more in this video. 

🔗 Link building has long been synonymous with guest posts and link insertions. However, the SEO landscape is evolving, and as AI-driven content becomes more prominent, the value of links is soaring. This surge in demand is leading to an increased focus on link building, but it also brings challenges.

🔄 The main issue with traditional link building methods is their replicability. If you can buy a link, so can your competitor. Plus, the growing demand for backlinks is turning many websites into link farms, diminishing the value of their links.

🌐 As a result, many are pivoting their strategies towards securing more unique and challenging links. Private Blog Networks (PBNs) are gaining traction as they offer greater control over various factors compared to traditional guest posting.

📢 Meanwhile, Digital PR is becoming a buzzword in the industry. It's about applying traditional PR tactics in the digital realm, focusing on high-quality link acquisition. Although I'm not an expert in digital PR, I'll share insights on leveraging it for SEO and obtaining those coveted high-quality links.

Key Strategies in Digital PR for SEO:

Reactive PR:
HARO (Help A Reporter Out) is a primary platform here. It's a space where journalists seek contributions for their articles. Quick and apt responses can land you spots on significant websites.
Try out platforms like Terkel, Help a B2B Writer, or SourceBottle.
It’s also a great way to make initial contacts for future outreach.
🚀 Special Announcement: Don't miss the early beta launch of my affordable SEO data tool, Clicks, happening next Thursday! The first 50 sign-ups get an exclusive preview. Find the waitlist link in the pinned comment below.

DATA Publishing:

This involves creating content like interactive maps, studies, infographics, and conducting surveys. These can attract media attention and backlinks.
Examples: Pantry and Larder's Interactive Map, Online Casino's Future Gamer Study, Backlinko's Data Studies.
News Jacking or Trend Jacking:

Quickly capitalizing on trending topics can garner attention and backlinks. Setting up alerts on Google and Twitter for specific terms can help you stay ahead.
Coining Terms:

This can be effective if you have a significant audience. Example: Rock Content's take on Inbound Marketing.
🔍 For Digital PR outreach, finding the right journalist is as crucial as crafting your pitch. Here are some resources:

Muckrack (though it can be pricey).
Lower-cost alternatives like Prowly by SEMrush, Journolink, and JournoFinder.

metadata.title: Digital PR: earn relevant links with data only you have
metadata.author: Iron Goo
metadata.shortDescription:
Earn relevant backlinks by giving journalists a finding they can turn into a story.
Learn how to score a digital PR idea, write a focused pitch and set realistic expectations before spending your budget.

- Five news values for judging ideas, including original data that makes your site a useful source.
- How data stories, regional maps and tangential angles compare on reach and relevance.
- What journalists reject, and how to pitch the finding with clear evidence and a credible method.
- Why focused outreach can outperform mass emails, and what realistic link results look like.
- Where earned links should point, how internal links pass value onward, and how to request missing links.
- How earned coverage connects to AI citations, what the research cannot prove, and why fabricated data undermines campaigns.

Free resources and the full transcript at https://irongoo.com/videos/digital-pr
Free ebook, Semantic SEO and AI Visibility: https://irongoo.com/ebook

#SEO #LinkBuilding #DigitalPR

That's across 86,000 real campaigns.
Most pitches are sent, ignored, and deleted with the speed of a reflex.
And yet digital PR is the one link building method Google's own search advocate
has praised in public.
In January 2021 he wrote that he loves some of what he sees from digital
PR, and that it's a shame it gets lumped in with the spammy kind.
So the method works.
The way most people run it doesn't.
So today we design a story a journalist actually wants, score it before
spending a cent, and fix a pitch live, using three ideas for our example
site, ReelRadar.
Then we set honest expectations, because most of the link counts you've
seen quoted are outliers.
Where this sits in the course: we're not the crowd that says every link
must be earned this way.
Other methods still work in many industries when they're run with precision,
and they have their own episodes.
Digital PR is the one you can run in the open, with your name on it, and
it pays twice: links for Google, and mentions that AI answers pick up.
Start from the other side of the inbox.
A journalist isn't looking for content.
A journalist is looking for a story the editor will run and the readers
will actually finish.
In a 2026 survey of journalists, 66% said they use material from PR people

Notice that none of these is about how famous your brand is.

So what makes a story fit?
We judge every idea against five news values.
Timeliness: why now, and not last year?
Surprise: does the finding go against what people assume?
Proximity: is it about the reader's city, country or community.
Human interest: is there a person or a feeling in it.
And the one most teams forget: data you own, something nobody else can publish

One warning on timeliness.

Build a campaign around a film's opening weekend, and if the film flops

Reactive stories can work very well, but they ship within days, and you
keep a backup angle in the drawer.

own headline.
And the tangential angle: a story only loosely about what you sell, which
sneaks a dull brand onto lifestyle and news pages.
Each shape has a trade-off.
Data stories are the most defensible and earn the most relevant links, but
they need real data and a finding that's actually interesting.
Maps multiply the audience, but local coverage is often off topic for your
site.
Tangential stories reach the widest press and earn the least relevant links.
Relevance matters here for the same reason it matters everywhere in this
course.
A link from a film site to a film site carries meaning.
A link from a recipe column to a film site carries much less.
So when we score ideas, reach is not the only thing on the sheet.
We also ask whether the people who would cover this story write about our
topic.
Now let's do it live.

films land on streaming.

Score it.

Surprise, possibly, if the gap really has changed, and we will only know

Proximity, no, it is the same story everywhere.
Human interest, weak.
Data we own, yes, and that is the one that matters most.
Nobody else has ReelRadar's records.
Three ticks, and the coverage would come from film and entertainment writers,
which is exactly where we want links.
Idea two, a map: which streaming genre each US state looks up most on ReelRadar.
Timely, only loosely.
Surprise, often, because people love to argue about their own state.
Proximity, very strong, every state paper gets a headline.
Human interest, yes.
Data we own, yes.
Four ticks, more than idea one.
The catch is relevance.
Much of that coverage would land on general news and lifestyle pages, not
film pages.
Idea three, tangential: what jobs famous film villains would do in real
life.
Human interest, yes, and it is fun.
Surprise, mild.
Timely, no.
Proximity, no.
Data we own, none.
It is an opinion piece with a costume on.
It might get picked up by a listicle site, but it has no data behind it

Our call: run idea one first.
It earns links from the press that covers our topic, and the data keeps

Hold idea two as the second campaign, built from the same data, to reach

Drop idea three unless someone finds real data for it.
The score sheet does not decide for you.

Now the pitch.
Here's a first draft of the email for idea one, written the way most pitches
get written.
Read it like a busy entertainment editor would, with one eye already on
the next email.
Everything journalists say they hate is in here.
The subject line is about us, not the story.
The first line is filler.
The second paragraph is pure promotion, which is exactly what 71% of journalists
said makes them hit reject.
And the finding, the only reason anyone would cover this, is never stated.
The editor has to click a link to discover whether there's a story at all.
Spoiler: they won't click.
Here is the rewrite.
The subject line is the finding, written the way a headline would be.
The first sentence states the number and where it came from.
The second line says why it matters now.
Then one line on method, so the journalist can trust it, and an offer: the

No adjectives about ourselves at all.
Notice the square brackets.
We left them empty on purpose, because this is a template, and the numbers

Then send it to people who cover this beat, checked against what they actually

Then the follow-up.
One polite nudge a few days later is normal.
Five nudges is how you end up in a journalist's group chat as a cautionary
tale.
If the story didn't land, the fix is usually the angle or the list, not

In the outreach data we opened with, campaigns sent to fifty to a hundred

Campaigns blasted to more than a thousand averaged under three and a half.

The spray-and-pray crowd is mostly praying.
Where does the link point?
Usually at the page that holds the study, not your homepage and not a money
page.
That is fine.
A good data page keeps earning links for years if you update it, and from

We covered how that routing works earlier in this part of the course.
And when someone covers the story without linking?
Don't panic and don't be pushy.
A short, friendly note pointing to the full data page, where readers can

Placebo.

Count the links, but report who gave them.

Paid and advertorial content?

Placebo. Nothing in the data we could verify supports 50 as a normal result. Expect a handful to a dozen good links from a well run campaign, with a long tail where a few take off. And eight links from the right film writers can be worth more than 80 from aggregator sites. Judge it by who linked, not just how many. Timing matters too. In a 2026 survey of more than 150 digital PR people, 81% said first coverage usually arrives within a week of launch, and 85% see measurable results within six months. Coverage is fast. The ranking effect is slow. Plan the report for both. The practitioners have moved on from counting, too. In the same survey, eighty five percent judge success by quality links, ahead of 71% who count total links, and 55% now track whether the coverage gets cited in AI answers. That's the right order. Count the links, but report who gave them. Claim number two: you need a big brand to get press. This one's harder to call. Big brands do get their emails opened more easily, and some industries are simply tougher. In that same survey, finance was named the hardest industry to earn links in, and travel the easiest. But look again at why journalists reject pitches. Wrong beat, too promotional, mass email. Not one of the top reasons is that they've never heard of you. A small site with data nobody else has isn't a nobody. It's a source. And a big brand with a press release about itself is just noise with a logo. Our verdict is contested: brand helps, the story decides, and in our own campaigns the angle has mattered more than the name on the email. Now the line you must not cross. Google's spam policy lists creating low value content mainly to manipulate linking signals as link spam. A survey you never ran, numbers you made up, an expert who doesn't exist: that's exactly what it describes. Journalists catch it too, and a correction on a news site is worse than no coverage at all. Same story with expert quote platforms. The best known reporter request service was renamed, then shut down by its owner at the end of 2024, and the brand was sold and relaunched by a new owner in April 2025. Platforms come and go. What lasts is being a real source: someone with real data or real experience who answers fast and gets it right. And here's why digital PR matters even more now. A May 2026 study of more than 25 million links cited by ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini found 84% came from earned media. Paid and advertorial content? A third of 1%. The coverage you earn with a real story is the kind AI answers read. Google's own 2026 guide adds the other half: chasing inauthentic mentions isn't as helpful as it might seem. One caution. That study shows what AI tools cite, not what causes a citation, and it comes from a company that sells PR software. We dig into what AI answers count in the next episode. For now: a campaign that earns real coverage builds links and the record AI answers read from, in one piece of work. So here's the episode on one screen. Digital PR works when you start from what a journalist needs, score the idea before you spend, and pitch the finding instead of yourself. Expect a handful of good links, not 50, and judge them by who linked. And never invent the data. That's the one move that turns the cleanest link method into spam. The campaign scoring sheet and the pitch template from this episode are free on the episode page at irongoo.com. Score your next idea on it before anyone writes a word of the press release.

💥 Join TOFU, the premier content marketing & SEO community with 2,500++ members, for FREE: http://JoinTOFU.co

 —

*Summary*

In this conversation, Tyler Hakes and Hyun Lee discuss using Haro for link building. They cover getting started, challenges, benefits, ROI, setting expectations, finding a good fit for pitches, credibility, creative fit, staying in your lane, and filtering by outlet. They also discuss the importance of PR links, choosing sites to pitch, do-follow and no-follow links, topical relevance, building relationships, avoiding pitching mistakes, crafting effective pitches, credibility and fit, creating a compelling signature, adding personality, pitch structure, timing, gaining an edge with early pitches, and managing workflow.

*Key Takeaways*

• Haro link building can be a valuable strategy for building high authority links to your website.
• It is important to set realistic expectations for Haro results and be prepared for a time investment.
• Finding a good fit for pitches is crucial, and it is important to stay in your niche and focus on pitches that align with your expertise.
• Establishing credibility in pitches is key, and leveraging your expertise and unique insights can help you stand out.
• Filtering by outlet can help ensure that you are targeting reputable publications and journalists. Getting links is important for SEO, but it's also important to consider the authority and relevance of the sites you pitch to.
• Do-follow links are generally preferred, but there can be exceptions depending on the opportunity and the goals of the client.
• Topical relevance is important, but there may be cases where a pitch that is not directly relevant can still be valuable if it's from a reputable publication.
• Building relationships with journalists is crucial for long-term success in PR and link building.
• Mistakes to avoid in pitching include sending irrelevant pitches, talking about your product or service too early, and using boring subject lines.
• Crafting effective pitches involves providing unique insights, data, and making it easy for journalists to use your pitch.
• Establishing credibility and fit is important in pitches, and adding personality to your pitch can help you stand out.
• The structure of a pitch should include a hook, a response to the query, and a compelling signature with relevant links.
• Timing is important in responding to queries, and early pitches can give you an edge over the competition.
• Managing your workflow and timing is crucial in effectively using HARO and other PR platforms.

metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re new to SEO and link building, this complete beginner’s tutorial will teach you the principles and strategies to get powerful and high-quality backlinks in 2020. 

***************************************
Additional Link Building Resources

7 Attributes of High Quality Backlinks ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E3mDlVutW_o&

How to Get Backlinks with Negotiation and Persuasion ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mxusD0K-IYA

Guest Posting at Scale: Get Tons of High Quality Backlinks ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aQK1Vbgb-RY

How to Build Unique Backlinks With Resource Page Link Building ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8f4YTubL6cM&list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2tjUTuAHpHidz5e2hAedP_m&index=5

Broken Link Building in Action (Strategies, Outreach Emails and Stats Revealed) ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOSrx95e4lo

Link Building Tutorials (Step-By-Step)  ► https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2tjUTuAHpHidz5e2hAedP_m

How to Get Backlinks By “Stealing” From Low-Quality Pages ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wPjPjNK-bDM&list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2tjUTuAHpHidz5e2hAedP_m&index=3

How to Find Someone’s Email Address (in Seconds) ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HA5tLHG80js&list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2tjUTuAHpHidz5e2hAedP_m&index=11

How to Write Outreach Emails (That Won’t Get Ignored) ► https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nAIWG8883uo&list=PLvJ_dXFSpd2tjUTuAHpHidz5e2hAedP_m&index=2
***************************************
Link building is arguably the most challenging part of SEO. It’s a part that requires technical prowess, a creative approach, and just straight up grit and grind. 

So what is link building? 

Here’s the standard definition. Link building is the process of getting other websites to link to a page on your website. And these hyperlinks are called backlinks. 

However, most people can’t seem to get the link building process right. This ultimately boils down to execution. 

The reason why execution is tough is because people focus too much on the end result, i.e. getting backlinks to their pages. The process is actually very relational. And relationships are built by humans, not “borrowed” templates from videos and blog posts. 

So, here’s a better definition: link building is the process of building relationships with other relevant site owners who want and will link to your content because it enhances theirs.

It includes relationships, relevance, and a value exchange.

Since link building is tough, you need to understand why it’s worth the effort. In short, backlinks are used by search engines like Google to help rank web pages. And the reason for this is something called PageRank. 

Why does PageRank matter and how does PageRank work? You’ll learn all about it in the video. 

Once you’ve understood how PageRank works, you’ll want to know how to get backlinks to your site. 

There are 3 ways to get them. 
► Create backlinks
► Buy backlinks
► Earn backlinks

Out of the three, only one of them is truly valuable. In the tutorial, you’ll learn which one that is. 

However, not all backlinks are good. Only some are really valuable. 

To understand what makes a link good, there are two main categories you should look at. 
► Relevance
► Authoritativeness

In the video, you’ll learn what these two concepts mean and how you can evaluate links for these two qualities. 

Once you’ve understood everything before this, you’ll want to know what link building strategies you can use. 

And in the video, we’ll share the link building strategies that actually work.

1:55 - What is PageRank
3:34 - How do you get backlinks
4:59 - How to define good backlinks
6:48 - What are Ahrefs Domain and URL ratings
7:23 - Hyperlink structure and attributes 
10:54 - Definition of a ‘linkable content’
12:52 - Importance of a ‘pitch’ for the outreach
15:38 - Guest blogging
16:31 - Resource page link building
17:38 - Broken link building
18:35 - Link building with HARO

In short, backlinks are used by search engines like Google to help rank web pages.
And it's been this way since 1998 when Google created PageRank.
PageRank is a mathematical formula that judges the "value of a page" by looking at the quantity and
quality of other pages that link to it.
And Google confirms the importance of backlinks on their "How search works" page.
Under their "Ranking useful pages" heading, they state:
"If other prominent websites on the subject link to the page, that's a good sign that
the information is of high quality."
We also found a clear correlation between organic traffic and backlinks from unique
websites in our study of over one billion web pages.
So while getting backlinks may be harder than let's say, creating a blog post, they're absolutely
critical if you want to rank for competitive phrases.
Now, you might be thinking...well, so and so said not to focus on link building because
high-quality content always attracts links.
Well, how do you get that content in front of people in the first place?
Unfortunately, the concept of "if you build it and they will come" is just pure fantasy.
Or you might have heard other people say
"I get tons of traffic without building backlinks, so no need to go through the struggle."
Yes, it's possible to rank pages without backlinks, but let me say this one more time.
Backlinks are absolutely critical, if you want to rank for competitive phrases.
And competitive phrases are usually the ones that'll drive the most traffic and revenue
for your business.
For example, queries related to SEO are extremely competitive, but they're also very lucrative.
And if you take a look at our blog's backlink growth in Ahrefs' Site Explorer, you'll see that
the growth curve almost mirrors that of our organic traffic.
They're rising together.
So how do you get backlinks?
Well, there are three ways to get them.
You can create them, buy them, or earn them.
Let's go through each method.
Creating backlinks means to manually add links to your site.
This can be done by adding your website to directories, leaving comments on blogs, or
adding a website to your social media profile.
Anyone can do this with minimal effort, so they're not that effective from an SEO and
ranking perspective.
Buying backlinks is exactly as it sounds.
You pay webmasters or authors a fee and in return, they'll link back to a page on your site.
Now, this is against Google's Webmaster Guidelines and can potentially result in a penalty.
That could be anything from losing ranking positions or even worse, getting your pages
removed from Google's search index.
Also, buying links isn't exactly cheap.
We contacted 250 websites to ask if they sell links.
And we found that the average cost of buying one was nearly $353.
And no, we didn't buy any.
The final way to get backlinks is to earn them.
And this is usually done by emailing other website owners and editors and asking them
to link to you.
This is the hardest method of the three, but generally speaking, the harder it is to obtain
a link, the more valuable it'll be.
And for that reason, we'll be focusing on earning backlinks through email outreach.
And I'll touch on a few tactics later.
Now, not all links are created equal.
Some will help propel your pages to the top of Google, while others can actually hurt your site.
So what makes a link actually good?
To simplify it as much as possible, there are two main categories you should look at.
First is relevance.
Ideally, you want to get backlinks from relevant websites and pages.
For example, let's say you have a page on the best USB microphones.
Getting a link from a page on the topic of video conferencing would be much more relevant than
a link on a page about gardening tips.
And this also plays out at the website level.
Getting a link from a tech site like Cnet would likely carry more weight than one
from a recipe site like All Recipes.
The second category is authoritativeness.
Now, if you're unfamiliar with "authority" in the context of link building, it basically
represents the so-called "link power" a web page has.
And this relates to how PageRank works.
As we discussed before, both the quantity and quality of links matter.
So the more quality links a page gets, the more PageRank it earns.
Now, PageRank doesn't appear out of thin air.
It comes from other pages.
This means that pages with authority, can pass it to other pages through hyperlinks.
So the more PageRank a linking page has, the more it can pass to those outbound links.
For example, let's say page C has two links: one from page A and one from page B.
Page A is stronger than page B and also has fewer outgoing links.
Feed this information into the PageRank algorithm, and you get the PageRank of page C.
Now, this is obviously a simplified version of how PageRank works, but the key point here
is that you want to get links from high-authority pages because they'll likely have the greatest
impact on your rankings.
Now, while Google doesn't provide PageRank or website authority scores, we have two metrics
at Ahrefs that try to quantify it.
Domain Rating is our website authority metric and it represents the overall strength of
a website's backlink profile.
And URL rating is our page-level authority metric, which represents the overall strength
of a Page's backlink profile.
We have a full video on assessing high-quality backlinks, so I'll link that up for you in the description.
Alright, so at this point, we've covered what link building is, why it's important, three methods to
get them, and some attributes of good-quality links.
What we haven't talked about yet, is the actual link itself.
So let's break down the anatomy of a hyperlink and the impact each part has on SEO.
Here's what a link looks like to your website visitors.
And if we look at the HTML code, then it would look like this.
Now, there are three basic parts to a link that matter in SEO.
The destination URL, anchor text, and the "rel" attribute or lack of one.
The destination URL is simply the URL the person will visit when the link is clicked.
The second part of a link is the anchor text.
The anchor text is the clickable word, phrase, or image attached to the link.
So in our example, Site Explorer is the anchor text, which is the name of our competitor
analysis tool.
Google uses anchor texts to better understand what a page is about and what terms it should
rank for.
But building lots of links with keyword-rich anchors is classified as a link scheme, and
may result in a Google penalty as it looks unnatural.
For example, if you had a post on the best wireless headphones and had a hundred links
pointing to it where the anchor texts were all "best wireless headphones," then it would
look quite unnatural.
People often use anchors such as the company's brand name, the title of the page, the URL, or
phrases like "click here."
And here's some proof.
If we look at the anchors of backlinks pointing to our data study on featured snippets, you'll see
varying anchor texts like "old studies," "ahrefs," "research," and even specific stats like "99.58%,"
"8.6% of all clicks," and so on.
In fact, there are only 14 websites that have linked to us using the anchor text "featured snippet."
With most earned links, you have very little or no control over the anchor text,
so over-optimization isn't something you really need to worry about.
And the last part is the "rel" attribute.
Some links contain a "rel" attribute, which is intended to tell crawlers the relationship
between the linking page and the linked page.
And the three "rel" values that you should know about when it comes to link building are "nofollow,"
"UGC," and "sponsored."
Historically, nofollow links told Google that the linking page would rather not associate
themselves with the linked page.
And for that reason, Google didn't transfer "authority" through those links.
But then Google added a couple other "rel" values: "UGC," which stands for "user-generated content,"
and "sponsored," which signifies a paid link.
They also announced that going forward, they would look at these link attributes as "hints,"
meaning, they may pass value through them at their discretion.
Now, if a link doesn't have any of these "rel" values, then it would be called a "followed" link.
Meaning, the link can pass PageRank and help boost your rankings.
Seeing as this is still relatively new, I'd recommend focusing on building "followed" links,
although that's only partially within your control.
One other thing I want to touch on is link placement.
Prominent links are more likely to be clicked, and it's believed that Google takes this into
account when determining how much authority a link transfers.
For instance, an editorial link is more likely to be clicked than a link in the footer.
So, all else being equal, the former would be better than the latter.
Alright, so by now, you should have a general overview of the more technical things that
are involved in link building.
But as I mentioned, there's also a creative part that's required.
And by creative, I'm talking about the content creative as well as getting creative with
your email pitch.
Now, with enough willpower and determination, it's possible to build links to any kind of page.
But life is a lot easier when you have something that people actually want to link to.
So let's talk about the content side of things first.
There are a couple of key attributes that linkable content has.
First, it's usually non-commercial.
Commercial content, like product pages from an ecommerce store or sales pages, are tougher
to get links to.
Why?
Because no one wants to contribute to your bank account without some kind of compensation
or at the very least, having first-hand experience with your products or services.
So by creating non-commercial content, with high utility, you're creating something that's
more deserving of a link.
That leads us into the second attribute.
Linkable content is helpful.
People want to link to helpful content because it directs their audience to resources that
complement their own.
And helpful content can be in all different forms.
For instance, well-written blog posts with factual information can get lots of links.
Healthline is a great example of this.
Their blog posts are usually concise and as far as I understand, many of their articles
are vetted by medical professionals.
As a result, all of their top linked-to pages are informational blog posts, which individually
have thousands of referring domains pointing at them.
Calculators and tools can also act as link magnets.
In fact, our free backlink checker has gotten over 2,000 links from unique websites.
Nerdwallet's retirement calculator has gotten over 800 links from unique websites.
And Bank Rate's mortgage calculator has over 3,500 links from unique websites.
Data-studies and case studies are also a great type of content that attracts links.
For example, our study on featured snippets has earned over 1,200 referring domains.
And it doesn't even need to be your own data.
This page has gotten 570 referring domains and it's just a curated list of stats on coffee.
Bottomline, if your content is a helpful resource for their audience or it supports arguments
they're making like a stat or fact, then your chances of earning backlinks increases.
Now, the second part to link building where creativity is required is the pitch.
Building links means you need to reach out to authors and editors and ask them to link to you.
Just like in sales, these people are called "prospects."
Now, it's called a "pitch" for a reason.
You can't just ask people to link to you without a good reason.
Let me put this into perspective.
Imagine someone showed up at your door and they asked you for money.
That's it.
You'd probably be speechless and just shut the door.
Now, if they told you that they were raising money for a good cause in your community,
you might consider listening to them.
And that brings us to the first part of the pitch.
You need to have a good reason to contact people.
Generally speaking, the better the reason, the higher your chance of achieving your goal.
So in that door knocker scenario, they might say something like…
"Hi Bobby, my name is Samantha and I'm a part of the Ahrefs' Tigers soccer team.
The reason I'm here is because our team recently lost funding so I'm trying to raise money to help
our team get new uniforms.
Since your daughter Felicity played on our team a few years ago, I thought you might
like to help."
I'm wondering if you'd like to donate $10, which will pay for half of one of the Tiger's uniforms?"
Now, if you were Bobby, would you give Samantha $10?
Maybe.
But another key point to note is that the pitch is personalized, which can also help
improve your link conversion rates.
Now, how do we take this pitch from a "maybe" to a "probably?"
Let's add on to Samantha's pitch.
"Since we're registered as a charitable organization, we'd be happy to provide a tax receipt for any
donations above $10."
Now the pitch has just gotten stronger and could even lead to higher valued donations.
And this brings us to the final part of the pitch and that's the value exchange.
Yes, some people will likely link to you if you have a good reason for contact and your
content matches the criteria we went through before.
But if they're getting something of value in exchange for a link, whether that be a resource
that adds value to their blog or free content from a guest post, then your chances of
getting a link increases.
But remember, things like exchanging links for money or doing excessive link exchanges
is against Google's Webmaster Guidelines.
The same goes for sending products to a person in exchange for a backlink.
So you'd need to get creative here to stay in line with the rules.
And I won't expand on this because it's just so highly situational based on the page you're
trying to build links to.
But we have a full video on using negotiation and persuasion for link building, so I'll link that
video up in the description.
Now, as you can see, link building is both an art and a science.
Pitches are also highly situational and will vary from person to person.
But there are quite a few link building strategies that are streamlined and have been proven
to work time and time again.
So let's go through some of these strategies and I'll explain what it is, why it works, and
how you can do them.
The first link building strategy is guest blogging.
Guest blogging is when you create content for another website.
And the reason why this strategy works is because there's a clear value exchange.
They get great content for free, and almost always, you should be able to get a link back
to your site; whether that be within the content or in the author bio.
So the way guest blogging works is to find other blogs in your industry, pitch and agree
on a relevant topic, and then you would write a post for them.
One way to find other industry blogs is with Ahrefs' Content Explorer.
Just search for a topic related to your niche.
Next, set the One page per domain filter since you don't need to pitch the same site multiple times.
You can then set a Domain Rating filter to something like 40-60 to find websites that
have decent website authority.
Export the results and start pitching.
The next link building tactic is called resource page link building.
This is where you get backlinks from web pages that curate and link out to useful
industry resources.
Now, this strategy works because the sole purpose of the pages' existence is to link
out to helpful and useful resources.
So if your content is great and you bring it to their attention, you're actually helping
them fulfill the page's purpose.
The basic process is simple.
First, you find industry resource pages, then you reach out to them and suggest
your resource for inclusion.
The easiest way to find relevant pages is to search in Google with a query like
intitle:resources inurl:resources.html and then a phrase related to your topic.
Visit the pages and see if they're actually resource
pages that link out to other external pages.
Then it's just a matter of reaching out to the ones you want to be mentioned on.
You can also use Ahrefs' SEO toolbar, which will show you important SEO metrics like Domain
Rating, URL rating, as well as both page and domain level search traffic estimations right
within the SERP.
The next link building strategy is broken link building.
Broken link building is a tactic where you find a dead link on a page, create your own
page on that topic, then ask everyone linking to the dead resource to link to your page instead.
The reason why it works is because webmasters who care about their site don't want to lead
their visitors to broken pages.
So oftentimes, they'll replace the dead link with yours.
Now, there are quite a few ways to find dead pages with backlinks.
The quickest way is to search for a topic in Ahrefs' Content Explorer, then filter for
broken pages.
Finally, set a referring domains filter with a minimum value of 10, which will show
pages with backlinks from at least 10 unique websites.
Now, after you've found a page, just click the caret, and then view it on archive.org.
This should show you the content that used to be on the dead page, which can help you
define your page's content angle.
Finally, click the caret, and go to the Backlinks report, where you can see all of the linking
pages to reach out to.
The next link building strategy is to use HARO.
HARO is a website that connects journalists with sources and sources with journalists.
Basically you'll get emails where journalists from media outlets are requesting information
on a specific topic.
Just filter through the topics and if you find something where you can add value,
respond to the journalist with your expert opinion.
And if they use you as a source, they'll usually link back to your site.
The value exchange here is simple.
You're exchanging your knowledge for a mention and usually a link from an authoritative site.
And there's no shortage of requests from mega publications like The Huffington Post, Forbes,
Inc, Entrepreneur, Reader's Digest, and the list goes on.
Now, I've only given you an overview of these tactics so I recommend watching some of
the tutorials in our link building playlist which will walk you through these tactics step-by-step.
And if you enjoyed this tutorial, make sure to like, share and subscribe for more actionable SEO and
marketing tutorials.
I'll see you in the next one.

Now, if you're unfamiliar with "authority" in the context of link building, it basically represents the so-called "link power" a web page has. And this relates to how PageRank works. As we discussed before, both the quantity and quality of links matter. So the more quality links a page gets, the more PageRank it earns. Now, PageRank doesn't appear out of thin air. It comes from other pages. This means that pages with authority, can pass it to other pages through hyperlinks. So the more PageRank a linking page has, the more it can pass to those outbound links. For example, let's say page C has two links: one from page A and one from page B. Page A is stronger than page B and also has fewer outgoing links. Feed this information into the PageRank algorithm, and you get the PageRank of page C. Now, this is obviously a simplified version of how PageRank works, but the key point here is that you want to get links from high-authority pages because they'll likely have the greatest impact on your rankings. Now, while Google doesn't provide PageRank or website authority scores, we have two metrics at Ahrefs that try to quantify it. Domain Rating is our website authority metric and it represents the overall strength of a website's backlink profile. And URL rating is our page-level authority metric, which represents the overall strength of a Page's backlink profile. We have a full video on assessing high-quality backlinks, so I'll link that up for you in the description. Alright, so at this point, we've covered what link building is, why it's important, three methods to get them, and some attributes of good-quality links. What we haven't talked about yet, is the actual link itself. So let's break down the anatomy of a hyperlink and the impact each part has on SEO. Here's what a link looks like to your website visitors. And if we look at the HTML code, then it would look like this. Now, there are three basic parts to a link that matter in SEO. The destination URL, anchor text, and the "rel" attribute or lack of one. The destination URL is simply the URL the person will visit when the link is clicked. The second part of a link is the anchor text. The anchor text is the clickable word, phrase, or image attached to the link. So in our example, Site Explorer is the anchor text, which is the name of our competitor analysis tool. Google uses anchor texts to better understand what a page is about and what terms it should rank for. But building lots of links with keyword-rich anchors is classified as a link scheme, and may result in a Google penalty as it looks unnatural. For example, if you had a post on the best wireless headphones and had a hundred links pointing to it where the anchor texts were all "best wireless headphones," then it would look quite unnatural. People often use anchors such as the company's brand name, the title of the page, the URL, or phrases like "click here." And here's some proof. If we look at the anchors of backlinks pointing to our data study on featured snippets, you'll see varying anchor texts like "old studies," "ahrefs," "research," and even specific stats like "99.58%," "8.6% of all clicks," and so on. In fact, there are only 14 websites that have linked to us using the anchor text "featured snippet." With most earned links, you have very little or no control over the anchor text, so over-optimization isn't something you really need to worry about. And the last part is the "rel" attribute. Some links contain a "rel" attribute, which is intended to tell crawlers the relationship between the linking page and the linked page. And the three "rel" values that you should know about when it comes to link building are "nofollow," "UGC," and "sponsored." Historically, nofollow links told Google that the linking page would rather not associate themselves with the linked page. And for that reason, Google didn't transfer "authority" through those links. But then Google added a couple other "rel" values: "UGC," which stands for "user-generated content," and "sponsored," which signifies a paid link. They also announced that going forward, they would look at these link attributes as "hints," meaning, they may pass value through them at their discretion. Now, if a link doesn't have any of these "rel" values, then it would be called a "followed" link. Meaning, the link can pass PageRank and help boost your rankings. Seeing as this is still relatively new, I'd recommend focusing on building "followed" links, although that's only partially within your control. One other thing I want to touch on is link placement. Prominent links are more likely to be clicked, and it's believed that Google takes this into account when determining how much authority a link transfers. For instance, an editorial link is more likely to be clicked than a link in the footer. So, all else being equal, the former would be better than the latter. Alright, so by now, you should have a general overview of the more technical things that are involved in link building. But as I mentioned, there's also a creative part that's required. And by creative, I'm talking about the content creative as well as getting creative with your email pitch. Now, with enough willpower and determination, it's possible to build links to any kind of page. But life is a lot easier when you have something that people actually want to link to. So let's talk about the content side of things first. There are a couple of key attributes that linkable content has. First, it's usually non-commercial. Commercial content, like product pages from an ecommerce store or sales pages, are tougher to get links to. Why? Because no one wants to contribute to your bank account without some kind of compensation or at the very least, having first-hand experience with your products or services. So by creating non-commercial content, with high utility, you're creating something that's more deserving of a link. That leads us into the second attribute. Linkable content is helpful. People want to link to helpful content because it directs their audience to resources that complement their own. And helpful content can be in all different forms. For instance, well-written blog posts with factual information can get lots of links. Healthline is a great example of this. Their blog posts are usually concise and as far as I understand, many of their articles are vetted by medical professionals. As a result, all of their top linked-to pages are informational blog posts, which individually have thousands of referring domains pointing at them. Calculators and tools can also act as link magnets. In fact, our free backlink checker has gotten over 2,000 links from unique websites. Nerdwallet's retirement calculator has gotten over 800 links from unique websites. And Bank Rate's mortgage calculator has over 3,500 links from unique websites. Data-studies and case studies are also a great type of content that attracts links. For example, our study on featured snippets has earned over 1,200 referring domains. And it doesn't even need to be your own data. This page has gotten 570 referring domains and it's just a curated list of stats on coffee. Bottomline, if your content is a helpful resource for their audience or it supports arguments they're making like a stat or fact, then your chances of earning backlinks increases. Now, the second part to link building where creativity is required is the pitch. Building links means you need to reach out to authors and editors and ask them to link to you. Just like in sales, these people are called "prospects." Now, it's called a "pitch" for a reason. You can't just ask people to link to you without a good reason. Let me put this into perspective. Imagine someone showed up at your door and they asked you for money. That's it. You'd probably be speechless and just shut the door. Now, if they told you that they were raising money for a good cause in your community, you might consider listening to them. And that brings us to the first part of the pitch. You need to have a good reason to contact people. Generally speaking, the better the reason, the higher your chance of achieving your goal. So in that door knocker scenario, they might say something like… "Hi Bobby, my name is Samantha and I'm a part of the Ahrefs' Tigers soccer team. The reason I'm here is because our team recently lost funding so I'm trying to raise money to help our team get new uniforms. Since your daughter Felicity played on our team a few years ago, I thought you might like to help." I'm wondering if you'd like to donate $10, which will pay for half of one of the Tiger's uniforms?" Now, if you were Bobby, would you give Samantha $10? Maybe. But another key point to note is that the pitch is personalized, which can also help improve your link conversion rates. Now, how do we take this pitch from a "maybe" to a "probably?" Let's add on to Samantha's pitch. "Since we're registered as a charitable organization, we'd be happy to provide a tax receipt for any donations above $10." Now the pitch has just gotten stronger and could even lead to higher valued donations. And this brings us to the final part of the pitch and that's the value exchange. Yes, some people will likely link to you if you have a good reason for contact and your content matches the criteria we went through before. But if they're getting something of value in exchange for a link, whether that be a resource that adds value to their blog or free content from a guest post, then your chances of getting a link increases. But remember, things like exchanging links for money or doing excessive link exchanges is against Google's Webmaster Guidelines. The same goes for sending products to a person in exchange for a backlink. So you'd need to get creative here to stay in line with the rules. And I won't expand on this because it's just so highly situational based on the page you're trying to build links to. But we have a full video on using negotiation and persuasion for link building, so I'll link that video up in the description. Now, as you can see, link building is both an art and a science. Pitches are also highly situational and will vary from person to person. But there are quite a few link building strategies that are streamlined and have been proven to work time and time again. So let's go through some of these strategies and I'll explain what it is, why it works, and how you can do them. The first link building strategy is guest blogging. Guest blogging is when you create content for another website. And the reason why this strategy works is because there's a clear value exchange. They get great content for free, and almost always, you should be able to get a link back to your site; whether that be within the content or in the author bio. So the way guest blogging works is to find other blogs in your industry, pitch and agree on a relevant topic, and then you would write a post for them. One way to find other industry blogs is with Ahrefs' Content Explorer. Just search for a topic related to your niche. Next, set the One page per domain filter since you don't need to pitch the same site multiple times. You can then set a Domain Rating filter to something like 40-60 to find websites that have decent website authority. Export the results and start pitching. The next link building tactic is called resource page link building. This is where you get backlinks from web pages that curate and link out to useful industry resources. Now, this strategy works because the sole purpose of the pages' existence is to link out to helpful and useful resources. So if your content is great and you bring it to their attention, you're actually helping them fulfill the page's purpose. The basic process is simple. First, you find industry resource pages, then you reach out to them and suggest your resource for inclusion. The easiest way to find relevant pages is to search in Google with a query like intitle:resources inurl:resources.html and then a phrase related to your topic. Visit the pages and see if they're actually resource pages that link out to other external pages. Then it's just a matter of reaching out to the ones you want to be mentioned on. You can also use Ahrefs' SEO toolbar, which will show you important SEO metrics like Domain Rating, URL rating, as well as both page and domain level search traffic estimations right within the SERP. The next link building strategy is broken link building. Broken link building is a tactic where you find a dead link on a page, create your own page on that topic, then ask everyone linking to the dead resource to link to your page instead. The reason why it works is because webmasters who care about their site don't want to lead their visitors to broken pages. So oftentimes, they'll replace the dead link with yours. Now, there are quite a few ways to find dead pages with backlinks. The quickest way is to search for a topic in Ahrefs' Content Explorer, then filter for broken pages. Finally, set a referring domains filter with a minimum value of 10, which will show pages with backlinks from at least 10 unique websites. Now, after you've found a page, just click the caret, and then view it on archive.org. This should show you the content that used to be on the dead page, which can help you define your page's content angle. Finally, click the caret, and go to the Backlinks report, where you can see all of the linking pages to reach out to. The next link building strategy is to use HARO. HARO is a website that connects journalists with sources and sources with journalists. Basically you'll get emails where journalists from media outlets are requesting information on a specific topic. Just filter through the topics and if you find something where you can add value, respond to the journalist with your expert opinion. And if they use you as a source, they'll usually link back to your site. The value exchange here is simple. You're exchanging your knowledge for a mention and usually a link from an authoritative site. And there's no shortage of requests from mega publications like The Huffington Post, Forbes, Inc, Entrepreneur, Reader's Digest, and the list goes on. Now, I've only given you an overview of these tactics so I recommend watching some of the tutorials in our link building playlist which will walk you through these tactics step-by-step. And if you enjoyed this tutorial, make sure to like, share and subscribe for more actionable SEO and marketing tutorials. I'll see you in the next one.

metadata.title: Digital PR: A New Fad or the Future of SEO?
metadata.author: LinkBuilding HQ
metadata.shortDescription:
What is digital PR, and what’s all the hype? Digital PR helps you get covered online - in articles, blogs, podcasts, and social posts -so your brand earns trust, traction, traffic, and quality backlinks. 

In this video, we discuss Digital PR, how it’s different from link building, and simple ways to get real coverage that helps your brand and SEO. 
You’ll see how stories, data, and smart outreach turn into mentions, engagement, traffic, and quality backlinks.

What you’ll learn

- What Digital PR is: a way to shape how people see your brand using online coverage.

- Digital PR vs. link building: brand visibility vs. keyword targeting and why both matter, but they’re not the same.

- What journalists want: expertise, data, and a clear story (and how to give it to them).

- Three coverage routes: Reactive PR (join the conversation), Passive PR (be findable), Inbound PR (publish assets journalists discover).

- A small-business example: Burger Revolution’s “Comment of the Day”: user-generated content done right.

-Metrics that matter: mentions, sentiment, traffic, backlinks (follow + nofollow), and leads/sales.


Chapters:
00:00 - Intro
00:21 - What is Digital PR
00:39 - The Differences between Traditional PR and Digital PR
00:51 - Strategic Storytelling with Digital PR
02:14 - How to Tell a Compelling Story
02:39 - How Digital PR Boosts Your Visibility
03:23 - Why the Buzz Around Digital PR?
03:47 - Are Link Building and Digital PR the Same Thing?
04:44 - How to Get Media Coverage
05:12 - How to Get Journalists to Notice You
05:47 - Alternate Approaches to Generate Buzz
06:44 - Burger Revolution's "Comment of the Day" Campaign
07:32 - Three Takeaways from the Campaign
07:54 - How to Show ROI on Digital PR
08:39 - Types and Relevancy of Links Matter
08:57 - The Most Important Metric
09:19 - Conclusion



If this helped, like the video, subscribe, and tap the bell for more tutorials and insights on Digital PR, link building, SEO, and content that earns coverage.

#DigitalPR #SEO #LinkBuilding #EarnedMedia #ContentMarketing #PR

segments.text: You've probably heard of the term
digital PR. People are saying it's the
next big thing, the only marketing
strategy you'll ever need. A real
gamecher.
But what is it and how can you get in on
the action? Digital PR is a promotional
strategy that uses various online
platforms to influence how your brand is
perceived. It combines media outreach,
social media engagement, influencer
collaboration, and highquality content
to create buzz and drive results. Now,
public relations in the traditional
sense was all about getting into a
newspaper or on television because
that's how people consumed their
information and how you could reach your
audience. Digital PR is that same sort
of thing, connecting with your audience,
but it's done through online channels.
Traditional PR used offline channels to
maintain a company's reputation and to
control its narrative. You'd pitch to
journalists and hope for positive
coverage in newspapers or television or
radio. And this is essentially one-way
communication. Whereas digital PR
thrives on engagement, likes, shares,
comments, and when your story is picked
up online and linked back to your site,
you gain valuable backlinks that boost
your SEO. Measuring the result of
digital PR is also more simplified
compared to the old way of doing things,
especially since we now have tools like
medium monitoring platforms and
analytics dashboards that let you
measure backlinks, traffic, and
engagement with precision. Digital PR is
fundamentally about strategic
storytelling.
As Seth Goden famously said, "People
don't buy goods and services. They buy
relationships, stories, and magic."
Great PR in almost every instance is
about telling compelling stories.
Whether it's your company's narrative,
your personal story, or the stories of
your customers,
it involves taking a step back and
examining your business from an external
standpoint.
Figure out what stories you have to tell
and then how can you present them in a
way that resonates with your target
audience. The approach is holistic and
long-term and it's actually kind of
simple. It prioritizes proactive brand
building over short-term tweaks and
reactive fixes. The great thing about
digital media is that your story doesn't
just disappear. It lives on in
searchable archives. So, it's always
there for people to find and for new
audiences to discover. Ongoing
discoverability is a key driver to the
effectiveness of digital PR. Let's say
your skin care brand lands a feature on
a beauty influencers blog. That blog
post residing permanently online
includes a no follow link back to your
site, sparks chatter on Instagram, and
it gets you a flood of traffic to your
site. This third-party validation acts
as a social proof and has the ability to
significantly influence consumer
behavior. So why the buzz all of a
sudden? Well, search engines are getting
more sophisticated. They go for that
high quality authoritative content and
are less tolerant towards manipulative
tactics. Digital PR is all about
building brand authority by getting back
links from reputable sites and managing
and enhancing a brand's reputation with
online reviews and social media
mentions. Now, link building and digital
PR are not the same thing. It's true you
can get a backlink from digital PR, but
that's just a superficial comparison.
Link building is a part of digital PR,
but they're not synonymous.
The main difference being link building
targets keywords while digital PR
targets brands. Link building involves
specific outreach targeting specific
keywords and its success is measured
based on the quality of the backlinks
acquired and the change in the website's
SER ranking. Digital PR is all about
building brand visibility and its
success is measured in media mentions,
brand sentiment, website traffic, social
media engagement, and ultimately
business leads and sales.
In digital PR, backlinks are a valuable
byproduct, but not the sole objective.
Contrary to what some business owners
believe, you don't necessarily need to
be a flashy, trendy company to get media
coverage, journalists often look for
three main elements: expertise, data,
and compelling stories. Understand what
stories journalists are already telling.
It's called media trend analysis. Figure
out what's hot, what's getting
attention, and what information
journalists are actively looking for.
For example, if everyone's talking about
remote work, journalists are looking for
data on its impact on productivity,
employee well-being, and team dynamics.
Once you know what they're looking for,
create the research that gives them
those insights. Conduct a survey,
analyze data, or partner with experts.
The key is to uncover something new, a
fresh angle, a surprising statistic, or
a counterintuitive finding.
This gives journalists a compelling
reason to tell your story.
But you don't always have to build
everything from the ground up. Another
effective approach is piggybacking on a
trending topic or a social trend.
Sometimes a clever twist on something
familiar or a touch of personalization
is all that you need to drum up some
interest to generate buzz. Here are some
ways to get your story out there.
Reactive PR. Engage in existing
conversations.
Offer your expertise to journalists
already covering related topics.
Passive PR. Make yourself available to
journalists when they're searching for
experts or data. Inbound PR. Optimize
your online content so journalists can
easily find your research when they're
searching online. Find out what stories
journalists are telling. create the data
that makes those stories better and then
make it easy for them to find you.
That's how you get featured. A good
example of a simple idea that generated
quite a bit of buzz online was Burger
Revolution's comment of the day
campaign. The Canadian-based burger
joint encouraged customers to jot down
their dining experience onto sticky
notes, which were then featured daily on
their social media pages. And it was
effective in boosting their following on
Facebook, Instagram, and X. A simple and
authentic approach that focused on
genuine customer interaction. No huge ad
budget, no complicated tech, just a
corkboard and some post-it notes.
Customer interaction amplified by social
media. The handwritten comments made a
powerful emotional connection far more
persuasive than any ad campaign. Three
takeaways from Burger Revolution.
Utilize user generated content.
Authentic customer voices are more
powerful than any manufactured hype.

It combines media outreach, social media engagement, influencer collaboration, and highquality content to create buzz and drive results. Now, public relations in the traditional sense was all about getting into a newspaper or on television because that's how people consumed their information and how you could reach your audience. Digital PR is that same sort of thing, connecting with your audience, but it's done through online channels. Traditional PR used offline channels to maintain a company's reputation and to control its narrative. You'd pitch to journalists and hope for positive coverage in newspapers or television or radio. And this is essentially one-way communication. Whereas digital PR thrives on engagement, likes, shares, comments, and when your story is picked up online and linked back to your site, you gain valuable backlinks that boost your SEO. Measuring the result of digital PR is also more simplified compared to the old way of doing things, especially since we now have tools like medium monitoring platforms and analytics dashboards that let you measure backlinks, traffic, and engagement with precision. Digital PR is fundamentally about strategic storytelling. As Seth Goden famously said, "People don't buy goods and services. They buy relationships, stories, and magic." Great PR in almost every instance is about telling compelling stories. Whether it's your company's narrative, your personal story, or the stories of your customers, it involves taking a step back and examining your business from an external standpoint. metadata.title: Google's CRACKDOWN on Parasite SEO: Why the EU is Probing Site Reputation Abuse
metadata.author: UltraSEOSolutions
metadata.shortDescription:
The European Commission has launched an investigation into Google's controversial policy targeting "parasite SEO," also known as "site reputation abuse," where third parties leverage authoritative websites to rank commercial content for competitive keywords.

This video breaks down the debate: why Google says it's protecting users from low-value, commercially motivated content, and why the EU claims the enforcement unfairly harms news publishers who rely on these partnerships to support their business.

We look at real-world impacts, including major publishers seeing traffic drop by 50-60% after being penalized for excessive third-party SEO content. This story reveals tensions around search quality, fair competition, and the financial reality facing publishers today.

Read Post: https://www.ultraseosolutions.com/googles-parasite-seo-crackdown-faces-eu-probe/

Thanks to Google's NotebookLM for making this video production possible.

metadata.title: How to Sell Listings on a Directory Website with Little or No Traffic
metadata.author: Ideal Directories
metadata.shortDescription:
Here at Ideal Directories, one of the concerns we hear from people looking to start their own business directory website is: How will I sell listings on my site when I’m just starting out and I don’t have a lot of website traffic?

That’s a legitimate concern….but an easy one to overcome. Here’s what you can do if a potential advertiser asks you about the traffic your getting to your site: 

First, acknowledge that you don't have a lot of traffic, but talk about your traffic goals. 

Next, discuss your plans to market the site, including anything and everything you're considering doing. 

Make sure you highlight the fact that your current pricing reflects the fact that you don't have a ton of traffic - and offer to lock your clients into your introductory rate. 

Finally, it's important to recognize that people don't just buy into your site – they buy into YOU. Speak to them about your passion for the community and helping small businesses flourish. 

Don't let the concern of selling listings on a site that's brand new stop you from getting started now.
